<div class="page-hero">
  <div class="genre-tag">Thriller / Psychological</div>
  <h1>Gone Girl</h1>
  <p class="subtitle">Book (2012) vs. Movie (2014) &mdash; dir. David Fincher</p>
</div>

<div class="page-wrap">
  <div class="comparison">
    <div class="panel-book">
      <div class="panel-label">The Book</div>
      <a class="book-cover-link" href="https://amzn.to/4e0alsg" target="_blank" rel="noopener sponsored">
        <img class="book-cover" src="./images/gone-girl.jpg" alt="Gone Girl book cover Gillian Flynn 2012" loading="lazy">
      </a>
      <a class="buy-btn" href="https://amzn.to/4e0alsg" target="_blank" rel="noopener sponsored">Buy the Book &rarr;</a>
      <p class="affiliate-disclosure">As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="panel-film">
      <div class="panel-label">The Movie</div>
      <a class="trailer-link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0VGD_jLyE9Y" target="_blank" rel="noopener">
        <div class="trailer-thumbnail">
          <img src="https://img.youtube.com/vi/0VGD_jLyE9Y/hqdefault.jpg" alt="Gone Girl 2014 film dir. David Fincher official trailer">
          <div class="trailer-play">▶</div>
        </div>
      </a>
      <p class="trailer-note">Starring Ben Affleck, Rosamund Pike, Neil Patrick Harris</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="meta-strip">
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Author</strong>Gillian Flynn</div>
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Book Published</strong>2012</div>
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Film Released</strong>2014</div>
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Director</strong>David Fincher</div>
    <span class="verdict-badge verdict-book">Book Wins</span>
  </div>

  <div class="body-text">
    <h2>The Story in Brief</h2>
    <p>On the morning of their fifth wedding anniversary, Nick Dunne's wife Amy goes missing. What follows is a media circus, a deteriorating marriage laid bare in Amy's diary entries, and a husband who keeps lying about things that turn out to matter. Gillian Flynn's novel alternates between Nick's present-tense account and Amy's past-tense diary &mdash; a structure that weaponizes the reader's trust. David Fincher, working from Flynn's own screenplay, made one of the decade's sharpest studio thrillers. The question is how much the translation cost.</p>

    <h2>Key Differences</h2>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>Amy's voice</h3>
      <p>The novel's greatest achievement is Amy's narration &mdash; razor-sharp, unreliable, and wickedly funny. Flynn gives her one of the most distinctive interior voices in contemporary fiction. The famous "Cool Girl" monologue is devastating on the page, a sustained piece of cultural criticism delivered by a sociopath. In the film, Rosamund Pike delivers it in voiceover and it lands &mdash; but compressed into two minutes, it loses the cumulative dread that builds across hundreds of pages of diary entries.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>Nick's culpability</h3>
      <p>The book spends considerably more time establishing Nick as genuinely complicit in the marriage's collapse &mdash; his selfishness, his condescension, his affair conducted with particular carelessness. Flynn wants you to understand why Amy hates him before you understand what Amy is. Affleck plays Nick as likeable-but-weak, which softens the moral ambiguity the novel carefully constructs.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>The diary structure</h3>
      <p>Flynn's dual timeline &mdash; Nick in the present, Amy's diary entries in the past &mdash; is the novel's central trick. The reader is lulled into trusting Amy's account before the twist recontextualizes everything. The film handles this reasonably well visually, but the intimacy of reading someone's private thoughts is irreplaceable. The twist hits harder on the page precisely because you've been inside Amy's head believing her.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>Desi Collings</h3>
      <p>Neil Patrick Harris is effectively cast against type, but the film trims Desi's backstory significantly. The novel establishes his obsessive devotion to Amy over years of correspondence and behavior; in the film he arrives already sinister. Some of the horror of Amy's final act depends on understanding how completely she has manipulated someone who genuinely loved her.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>The ending</h3>
      <p>Both versions end in the same place &mdash; Nick trapped, Amy pregnant, the performance of marriage continuing indefinitely &mdash; but the film rushes toward it. The novel's final pages are among Flynn's best writing: two people who despise each other, chained together, both too smart and too proud to blink first. It earns its bleakness in a way a two-hour film simply cannot.</p>
    </div>

    <h2>Should You Read First?</h2>
    <p>Yes, but the film works as a standalone in a way few adaptations do &mdash; Fincher and Flynn together is a strong enough combination that you won't feel cheated. That said, if you read the novel first, the film becomes a fascinating exercise in what survives translation: the plot survives intact, the atmosphere survives, Rosamund Pike is extraordinary. What doesn't survive is the slow erosion of trust that Flynn builds across four hundred pages. Read it first and the film rewards you. Watch it first and you'll still want to read the book.</p>

    <div class="verdict-box">
      <div class="verdict-title">Verdict</div>
      <p>Fincher's film is as good as a Gone Girl adaptation could possibly be &mdash; and it's still a lesser experience than the novel. Flynn's prose does something film cannot: it makes you complicit. You trust Amy. You root for her. Then you have to sit with what that says about you. Rosamund Pike is iconic, the film is gripping, and you should absolutely see it. But the book is the one that stays with you.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <h1>Animal Farm: Book vs Movie</h1>
  <p class="subtitle">George Orwell (1945 novella) vs Andy Serkis (2026 animated film) — Detailed comparison, key differences, and verdict</p>
</div>

<div class="page-wrap">
  <div class="comparison">
    <div class="panel-book">

      <p class="affiliate-disclosure">As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases.</p>
    </div>
    
    <div class="panel-film">
      <div class="panel-label">The Movie</div>
      <a class="trailer-link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=g8wLmj9SiKM" target="_blank" rel="noopener">
        <div class="trailer-thumbnail">
          <img src="https://img.youtube.com/vi/g8wLmj9SiKM/maxresdefault.jpg" alt="Animal Farm 2026 movie trailer thumbnail" loading="lazy">
          <div class="trailer-play">&#9658;</div>
        </div>
      </a>
      <p class="trailer-note">Directed by Andy Serkis • Theatrical release: May 1, 2026 (Angel Studios) • Voice cast includes Seth Rogen, Glenn Close, Kieran Culkin, Woody Harrelson</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="meta-strip">
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Author</strong> George Orwell</div>
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Book Published</strong> 1945 (Novella, ~80 pages)</div>
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Film Release</strong> May 1, 2026 (Theatrical)</div>
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Director</strong> Andy Serkis</div>
    <span class="verdict-badge verdict-book">Book Wins</span>
  </div>

  <div class="body-text">
    <h2>The Story in Brief (Spoiler-Free)</h2>
    <p>The animals of Manor Farm rebel against their human owner, dreaming of a society where all are equal. Under the leadership of the pigs, the revolution gradually corrupts into a new form of tyranny. Orwell’s 1945 novella is a razor-sharp political allegory that packs an entire history of failed revolutions into under 30,000 words. Andy Serkis’s 2026 animated adaptation brings the farm to life with modern animation and a star-studded voice cast, updating the themes for contemporary audiences.</p>

    <h2>Key Differences</h2>
    
    <div class="difference">
      <h3>The Allegory & Political Specificity</h3>
      <p>Orwell’s book is a precise satire of the Russian Revolution and Stalin’s rise: pigs = Bolsheviks, Napoleon = Stalin, Snowball = Trotsky. Serkis’s film broadens the allegory toward general authoritarianism and populist demagoguery, making it feel timely but losing some of the original’s historical sharpness.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>Prose Economy vs Expanded Runtime</h3>
      <p>The novella is famously efficient — every sentence serves the argument. The film expands brief moments into full set pieces, which adds visual flair but sometimes dilutes the relentless pacing that makes the book so powerful.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>Squealer the Propagandist</h3>
      <p>One of the book’s most chilling creations. The film gives Squealer more screen time and overt menace, but Orwell’s subtle, gaslighting version is often more terrifying because it mirrors real-world manipulation so quietly.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>Boxer’s Tragedy</h3>
      <p>The loyal carthorse who “works harder” is heartbreaking in both. The movie benefits from strong voice acting that makes his decency audible, but the book’s sparse prose makes his fate hit even harder.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>The Ending</h3>
      <p>Both reach the same devastating conclusion with animals unable to tell pigs from men. Orwell’s final sentence is one of literature’s most perfect gut punches. The film delivers appropriate gravity but can’t match the novella’s linguistic precision.</p>
    </div>

    <!-- New sections for depth -->
    <h2>Comparison Table</h2>
    <table>
      <thead><tr><th>Aspect</th><th>Book (1945)</th><th>Movie (2026)</th><th>Winner</th></tr></thead>
      <tbody>
        <tr><td>Allegory Precision</td><td>Highly specific to Stalinism</td><td>Broadened to modern authoritarianism</td><td>Book</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Pacing & Economy</td><td>Extremely tight (~2-hour read)</td><td>Feature-length with expanded scenes</td><td>Book</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Emotional Impact (Boxer)</td><td>Devastating in its brevity</td><td>Strong voice performances</td><td>Book</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Visual Experience</td><td>Relies on imagination</td><td>Modern animation & star cast</td><td>Movie</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Timelessness</td><td>Still taught in schools worldwide</td><td>Updated for 2026 audiences</td><td>Book</td></tr>
      </tbody>
    </table>

    <h2>Should You Read the Book First?</h2>
    <p><strong>Yes — strongly recommended.</strong> At just 80 pages, the novella takes most readers 1.5–2 hours. Orwell’s prose and compression are the core experience. Reading first makes the film a fascinating companion piece rather than a replacement. It’s one of the most efficient “read first” recommendations possible.</p>

    <div class="verdict-box">
      <div class="verdict-title">Final Verdict</div>
      <p>Orwell wrote one of the essential political texts of the twentieth century in the form of a children’s fable. Serkis’s 2026 adaptation is sincere and visually accomplished, but the novella remains irreplaceable. <strong>The book wins.</strong> Read it first — it takes an evening and lasts a lifetime.</p>
    </div>

    <!-- New: Reader value & engagement -->
    <h2>For Students, Teachers & Book Clubs</h2>
    <p>This comparison works especially well for classroom discussion. Key topics: power and corruption, the role of propaganda, and how revolutions can betray their ideals.</p>
  </div>

  <p class="subtitle">Book (2020) vs. Movie (2026) &mdash; dir. Chlo&eacute; Zhao</p>

<div class="page-wrap">
  <div class="comparison">
    <div class="panel-book">
      <div class="panel-label">The Book</div>
      <a class="book-cover-link" href="https://amzn.to/4sTMWgU" target="_blank" rel="noopener sponsored">

    <div class="panel-film">
      <div class="panel-label">The Movie</div>
            <a class="trailer-link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xYcgQMxQwmk" target="_blank" rel="noopener">
        <div class="trailer-thumbnail">
          <img src="https://img.youtube.com/vi/xYcgQMxQwmk/maxresdefault.jpg" alt="Hamnet 2026 film Jessie Buckley official trailer">
          <div class="trailer-play">▶</div>

  <div class="meta-strip">
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Author</strong>Maggie O'Farrell</div>
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Book Published</strong>2020</div>
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Film Released</strong>2026</div>
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Director</strong>Chlo&eacute; Zhao</div>
    <span class="verdict-badge verdict-book">Book Wins</span>
  </div>

  <div class="body-text">
    <h2>The Story in Brief</h2>
    <p>Maggie O'Farrell's Booker Prize-winning novel imagines the life of Agnes Hathaway — the woman who married William Shakespeare — and the death of their eleven-year-old son Hamnet from plague in 1596. O'Farrell never names her protagonist "Shakespeare," keeping focus relentlessly on Agnes and the devastation of her loss. The film stars Jessie Buckley as Agnes and Paul Mescal as the unnamed playwright, with Chloé Zhao — coming off Nomadland — directing.</p>

    <h2>Key Differences</h2>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>Agnes's interiority</h3>
      <p>The novel's greatest achievement is its access to Agnes's inner world — her strange gifts, her grief, her fury at a husband who is always half-absent. O'Farrell's prose moves between past and present with the logic of grief rather than chronology, and that interiority is essentially untranslatable. The film necessarily makes Agnes more externally legible; her strangeness on the page comes from thinking, not behaviour.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>The plague chapter</h3>
      <p>The novel contains a five-page setpiece that follows the plague from a flea on a piece of silk across Europe to arrive at a child in Stratford — one of the most controlled and devastating passages in contemporary fiction. The film distributes this material across its structure rather than presenting it as a single devastating blow. It works, but it lands differently.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>Shakespeare's absence</h3>
      <p>O'Farrell's choice to never name her playwright character is a structural argument: this is Agnes's story, and the most famous writer in English history is a peripheral figure in his own family. The film honours this, but Mescal's screen presence inevitably draws attention. He cannot be as absent on film as the unnamed husband is on the page.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>Time and chronology</h3>
      <p>The novel moves fluidly between Agnes's girlhood, her marriage, and the days surrounding Hamnet's death — the structure mirrors how grief actually works, returning obsessively to certain moments. A linear film handles this non-linearity with more restraint, which makes the emotional accumulation feel more conventional even when the filmmaking is excellent.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>The ending</h3>
      <p>O'Farrell's final movement — Agnes watching the first performance of Hamlet, understanding what her husband has done with their son's name — is handled with significant restraint in the film. Both versions earn their ending, but the novel's is quieter and more devastating for it.</p>
    </div>

    <h2>Should You Read First?</h2>
    <p>Yes — Hamnet is O'Farrell at her peak, and it requires no prior knowledge of Shakespeare. It is simply one of the best novels of the past decade, and it reads quickly despite its emotional density. Read it first. Then watch Zhao and Buckley honour it.</p>

    <div class="verdict-box">
      <div class="verdict-title">Verdict</div>
      <p>The novel is a masterpiece of interiority that no film can fully replicate. Zhao's adaptation is made with real intelligence and care, and Buckley is extraordinary — but the book is doing something only a book can do. Read it first, then let the film show you what survived the translation.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

    <h3>More Comparisons</h3>

<div class="page-hero">
  <div class="genre-tag">Romance / Sports Drama / LGBTQ+</div>
  <h1>Heated Rivalry</h1>
  <p class="subtitle">Book (2019) vs. Show (2025) &mdash; created by Jacob Tierney &bull; HBO Max / Crave</p>
</div>

<div class="page-wrap">
  <div class="comparison">
    <div class="panel-book">

    </div>
    <div class="panel-film">
      <div class="panel-label">The Show</div>
      <a class="trailer-link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lKO26odltss" target="_blank" rel="noopener">
        <div class="trailer-thumbnail">
          <img src="https://img.youtube.com/vi/lKO26odltss/maxresdefault.jpg" alt="Heated Rivalry 2025 official trailer HBO Max">
          <div class="trailer-play">&#9658;</div>
        </div>
      </a>
      <p class="trailer-note">Created by Jacob Tierney &mdash; Starring Connor Storrie, Hudson Williams &mdash; HBO Max / Crave: 2025</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="meta-strip">
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Author</strong>Rachel Reid</div>
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Book Published</strong>2019</div>
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Show Released</strong>2025</div>
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Creator</strong>Jacob Tierney</div>
    <span class="verdict-badge verdict-tie">Too Close to Call</span>
  </div>

  <div class="body-text">
    <h2>The Story in Brief</h2>
    <p>Shane Hollander and Ilya Rozanov are two of the best hockey players in the world — and bitter rivals on opposing teams who have been drawn to each other for years. What starts as a secret arrangement between two men who refuse to acknowledge what they feel becomes a years-long story of love, denial, ambition, and the cost of living in a sport that wasn't built for people like them. Rachel Reid's 2019 novel is one of the most celebrated entries in her <em>Game Changers</em> series and among the most beloved hockey romances ever written. Jacob Tierney's 2025 HBO Max adaptation premiered to extraordinary reception — an 8.8 on IMDb, a cultural phenomenon, and a series that sent an entire new generation of viewers straight to Reid's backlist.</p>

    <h2>Key Differences</h2>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>Interior voice</h3>
      <p>The novel's central advantage is complete access to Shane and Ilya's internal lives — their denial, their rationalisation, their longing rendered with Reid's characteristic warmth and precision. The show loses this by definition. Connor Storrie and Hudson Williams give performances of real sensitivity, but the subtext the novel makes text is sometimes harder to read on screen. What you feel watching them is real; what you <em>know</em> reading Reid is different and deeper.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>The timeline</h3>
      <p>Reid's novel spans several years of Shane and Ilya's careers, with time jumps that give the romance genuine scope and weight. The show compresses and restructures this for six episodes — which works better than you might expect. Tierney uses the compression to tighten the emotional arc rather than lose it, and some of the novel's slower middle section actually benefits from the edit.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>The hockey world</h3>
      <p>Reid is meticulous about the texture of professional hockey — the locker rooms, the road trips, the physical culture, the specific isolation of being an outsider inside the sport. The show's production design and on-ice sequences are excellent, but the novel lives inside the sport in a way six episodes of television cannot fully replicate.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>Ilya's Russian identity</h3>
      <p>Ilya's background — his Russian upbringing, his complicated relationship with home and language, what it means to be who he is in the context he came from — is more fully developed in the novel. The show handles it thoughtfully but necessarily briefly. François Arnaud brings considerable depth to scenes the novel gives many more pages.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>The secondary characters</h3>
      <p>Reid's <em>Game Changers</em> world includes recurring characters whose histories add texture for readers who've come to the series in order. The show introduces these characters freshly, which works on its own terms but lacks the accumulated affection novel readers bring to Scott Hunter, Kip Grady, and the broader cast.</p>
    </div>

    <h2>Should You Read First?</h2>
    <p>Either order works genuinely well — this is one of the site's most comfortable either-order recommendations. The show is faithful enough that watching first loses relatively little. But reading first means every scene the show gives you arrives loaded with interior knowledge that performance can only approximate. Our preference: read first. If you watched first and are now reading — welcome, and the book is even better than you're hoping.</p>

    <div class="verdict-box">
      <div class="verdict-title">Verdict</div>
      <p>Rachel Reid's novel is a slow-burn romance of real precision and warmth — one of the best in its genre. Jacob Tierney's adaptation is one of the best book-to-screen translations of recent years: visually confident, excellently cast, and faithful to the source's emotional core. Both versions are essential. Read the book. Watch the show. This is one of the closest calls on the site — and unlike most close calls, there is no wrong answer.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

</header>

<div class="page-hero">
  <div class="genre-tag">Literary Fiction / Comedy</div>
  <h1>High Fidelity</h1>
  <p class="subtitle">Book (1995) vs. Movie (2000) &mdash; dir. Stephen Frears</p>
</div>

<div class="page-wrap">
  <div class="comparison">
    <div class="panel-book">
      <div class="panel-label">The Book</div>
      <a class="book-cover-link" href="https://amzn.to/4c1avi1" target="_blank" rel="noopener sponsored">
        <img class="book-cover" src="./images/high-fidelity.jpg" alt="High Fidelity book cover Nick Hornby 1995" loading="lazy">
      </a>
      <a class="buy-btn" href="https://amzn.to/4c1avi1" target="_blank" rel="noopener sponsored">Buy the Book &rarr;</a>
      <p class="affiliate-disclosure">As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="panel-film">
      <div class="panel-label">The Movie</div>
      <a class="trailer-link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OA9gPtWDiww" target="_blank" rel="noopener">
        <div class="trailer-thumbnail">
          <img src="https://img.youtube.com/vi/OA9gPtWDiww/maxresdefault.jpg" alt="High Fidelity 2000 film dir. Stephen Frears official trailer">
          <div class="trailer-play">&#9658;</div>
        </div>
      </a>
      <p class="trailer-note">Starring John Cusack, Iben Hjejle, Jack Black, Todd Louiso &mdash; Film: 2000</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="meta-strip">
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Author</strong>Nick Hornby</div>
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Book Published</strong>1995</div>
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Film Released</strong>2000</div>
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Director</strong>Stephen Frears</div>
    <span class="verdict-badge verdict-tie">Too Close to Call</span>
  </div>

  <div class="body-text">
    <h2>The Story in Brief</h2>
    <p>Rob Fleming runs a failing record shop in North London and has just been dumped by his girlfriend Laura. He responds by compiling a top five list of his worst break-ups, tracking down his exes to find out where he went wrong, and spending a great deal of time thinking about music instead of his own emotional life. Nick Hornby's 1995 novel is a first-person comedy about a particular kind of man — intelligent, self-aware enough to diagnose his own problems but not quite enough to solve them — and one of the defining works of 1990s literary fiction. Stephen Frears's 2000 film moves the story from London to Chicago, replaces Rob Fleming with Rob Gordon, and casts John Cusack in one of his best performances. It is one of the most successful transatlantic adaptations in cinema history.</p>

    <h2>Key Differences</h2>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>London vs Chicago</h3>
      <p>Hornby's novel is specifically set in North London — the geography, the class textures, the particular relationship between British men of that generation and American music all contribute to its atmosphere. Frears and Cusack moved the story to Chicago, which has its own music culture and its own specific flavour of self-aware urban cool. Remarkably, almost nothing is lost. The transposition works because Hornby's subject — a certain kind of emotionally avoidant man who uses culture as a shield — is not specifically British. He is universal enough to survive the crossing.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>Rob's direct address</h3>
      <p>The novel is written in Rob's first person — a confessional, self-deprecating voice that is aware of its own evasions. The film gives Cusack extended direct address to the camera — Rob talks to the audience as he talks to himself in the novel, explaining his situation, making his lists, rationalising his behaviour. This is exactly the right adaptation of the prose voice into cinematic terms. Cusack's delivery of these monologues is the film's greatest achievement.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>Jack Black as Barry</h3>
      <p>Barry — Rob's overbearing, music-obsessed shop assistant — is a supporting character in the novel, vivid but not central. Jack Black's performance made Barry one of the most memorable supporting characters in the film's era, and earned the role a prominence that somewhat shifts the story's balance. Black's Barry is funnier and more immediately likeable than Hornby's, which is a slight distortion of the novel's emotional architecture but an undeniable pleasure.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>The music</h3>
      <p>Hornby's novel is saturated with specific musical references — the records Rob stocks, the lists he compiles, the songs that mark his emotional history. The film uses licensed music throughout and includes a genuinely brilliant sequence in which Rob and his friends debate the merits of various songs while processing his grief. The soundtrack is impeccable. Both versions understand that the music is not decoration but argument — evidence of how Rob thinks and what he uses thinking for.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>Laura</h3>
      <p>Iben Hjejle plays Laura with a quality of weary intelligence — a woman who knows exactly what Rob is doing and has loved him anyway, for longer than she should. Hornby's Laura is rendered through Rob's partial and self-serving account of her, which makes her both more mysterious and more sympathetic than his version admits. The film's Laura is more fully present, which is warmer and slightly reduces the gap between Rob's version of events and the truth.</p>
    </div>

    <h2>Should You Read First?</h2>
    <p>Either order works — this is one of the most comfortable either-order recommendations on the site, alongside About a Boy. The film is so faithful in spirit that watching first loses almost nothing. Read first for the full texture of Hornby's prose and Rob's specific London voice. Watch first for Cusack's monologues and Jack Black's Barry. Both versions are essential.</p>

    <div class="verdict-box">
      <div class="verdict-title">Verdict</div>
      <p>Hornby wrote a novel about a man who uses music and lists to avoid feeling anything genuinely difficult. Frears and Cusack made a film that is as good — moving the story from London to Chicago without losing anything essential and finding the perfect visual equivalent for Rob's confessional first-person voice. One of the most successful transatlantic literary adaptations in cinema. A genuine tie. Read the novel. See the film. Make your own top five list of which you prefer.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

<div class="page-hero">
  <div class="genre-tag">Science Fiction / Comedy</div>
  <h1>The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy</h1>
  <p class="subtitle">Book (1979) vs. Movie (2005) &mdash; dir. Garth Jennings</p>
</div>

<div class="page-wrap">
  <div class="comparison">
    <div class="panel-book">

        <div class="trailer-thumbnail">

  <div class="meta-strip">
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Author</strong>Douglas Adams</div>
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Book Published</strong>1979</div>
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Film Released</strong>2005</div>
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Director</strong>Garth Jennings</div>
    <span class="verdict-badge verdict-book">Book Wins</span>
  </div>

  <div class="body-text">
    <h2>The Story in Brief</h2>
    <p>Arthur Dent's house is about to be demolished to make way for a bypass. This turns out to be the least of his problems: Earth is simultaneously demolished to make way for a hyperspace bypass, and Arthur escapes only because his friend Ford Prefect is an alien researcher for the titular encyclopaedia. What follows is a tour of a universe that is deeply strange, largely indifferent to human concerns, and funnier than it has any right to be. Douglas Adams began the story as a BBC radio series in 1978, adapted it into the novel in 1979, and spent twenty years trying to make it into a film — the 2005 version, directed by Garth Jennings, was released four years after Adams's death. It is a loving, imperfect tribute to material that resists being filmed.</p>

    <h2>Key Differences</h2>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>Adams's narrative voice</h3>
      <p>The novel's comedy is inseparable from Adams's prose style — the deadpan asides, the elaborate digressions, the narrative voice that treats the destruction of Earth with the same mild interest it brings to the question of what to have for lunch. This voice is the joke. The film uses Stephen Fry as the voice of the Guide itself, which is the right instinct, but the jokes that work on the page as prose — the extended footnotes about Vogon poetry, the philosophical asides about the nature of improbability — become something different when they have to be dramatised rather than read.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>Martin Freeman as Arthur Dent</h3>
      <p>Freeman is perhaps the most precisely correct casting decision in literary adaptation history. Arthur Dent is a man defined by mild bewilderment and the stubborn persistence of English ordinariness in the face of cosmic absurdity — Freeman embodies this completely. His Arthur is not the funniest thing in the film but he is the most right thing, the still point around which the universe's chaos revolves.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>The Vogons</h3>
      <p>The Vogons — the bureaucratic alien species responsible for Earth's demolition, and for the worst poetry in the universe — are rendered in the film as magnificent Jim Henson creature-shop creations, physically perfect embodiments of Adams's description. This is one area where the film's visual imagination adds something the prose can only describe. The Vogon sequences are the film at its best.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>The added romance plot</h3>
      <p>The film introduces a more developed romance between Arthur and Trillian — a storyline that does not have the same prominence in the novel and that feels grafted on to provide conventional emotional stakes. Adams's novel is not particularly interested in romance; the film's version of Trillian (Zooey Deschanel) is given more agency and more centrality than the source provides, which works for the film and slightly against the novel's specific flavour of cosmic indifference.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>The answer to everything</h3>
      <p>The revelation that the answer to life, the universe, and everything is forty-two works in the novel because Adams has built up to it through the specific rhythm of his prose — the absurdity of the question machine, the millions of years of waiting, the bathos of the answer. The film delivers the same punchline to a different rhythm and it still works, but the buildup is compressed and the joke is slightly less devastating.</p>
    </div>

    <h2>Should You Read First?</h2>
    <p>Yes — and this is among the most emphatic read-first recommendations on the site, because the prose voice is not just the delivery mechanism for the jokes but the jokes themselves. Read the novel and the film becomes a warm, well-cast companion. Watch the film first and you will enjoy it and miss everything that made readers love the source for forty years.</p>

    <div class="verdict-box">
      <div class="verdict-title">Verdict</div>
      <p>Adams wrote a novel whose comedy lives entirely in the prose — the asides, the digressions, the narrative voice that is itself the joke. The 2005 film is affectionate, well-cast, and fundamentally loses the mechanism. Read the book. See the film for Martin Freeman, who is Arthur Dent in the way that some actors simply are the character. The novel is the real universe. The film is a pleasant tour of it.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

    <h3>More Comparisons</h3>

<div class="page-hero">
  <div class="genre-tag">Dystopian Fiction</div>
  <h1>Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping</h1>
  <p class="subtitle">Book (2025) vs. Movie (2026) &mdash; dir. Francis Lawrence</p>
</div>

<div class="page-wrap">
  <div class="comparison">
    <div class="panel-book">
      <div class="panel-label">The Book</div>
      <a class="book-cover-link" href="https://amzn.to/415ZN3r" target="_blank" rel="noopener sponsored">
        <img class="book-cover" src="./images/hunger-games-sunrise.jpg" alt="Hunger Games Sunrise on the Reaping book cover Suzanne Collins 2025" loading="lazy">
      </a>
      <a class="buy-btn" href="https://amzn.to/415ZN3r" target="_blank" rel="noopener sponsored">Buy the Book &rarr;</a>
      <p class="affiliate-disclosure">As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="panel-film">
      <div class="panel-label">The Movie</div>
            <a class="trailer-link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MPjxijuBuSo" target="_blank" rel="noopener">
        <div class="trailer-thumbnail">
          <img src="https://img.youtube.com/vi/MPjxijuBuSo/maxresdefault.jpg" alt="Hunger Games Sunrise on the Reaping 2026 film Ralph Fiennes official trailer">
          <div class="trailer-play">▶</div>
        </div>
      </a>
      <p class="trailer-note">Starring Joseph Zada, Ralph Fiennes, Elle Fanning &mdash; In theaters November 20, 2026</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="meta-strip">
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Author</strong>Suzanne Collins</div>
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Book Published</strong>2025</div>
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Film Released</strong>2026</div>
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Director</strong>Francis Lawrence</div>
    <span class="verdict-badge verdict-tie">It's a Tie</span>
  </div>

  <div class="body-text">
    <h2>The Story in Brief</h2>
    <p>Suzanne Collins returns to Panem for a second prequel, following a young Haymitch Abernathy — the District 12 tribute who will one day become Katniss Everdeen's dissolute but brilliant mentor. Set during the 50th Hunger Games, known as the Second Quarter Quell, Sunrise on the Reaping is Collins's most overtly political work: an interrogation of how authoritarian systems manufacture consent, erase memory, and punish resistance. Knowing where Haymitch ends up gives everything he does here an extra weight.</p>

    <h2>Key Differences</h2>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>Haymitch's trauma arc</h3>
      <p>The novel has room to follow Haymitch across years — his Games victory, the aftermath, the slow erosion that turns a clever survivor into the wreck Katniss first meets. Several chapters of processing and deterioration are necessarily compressed in the film, which means the connection between what we see here and the Haymitch of the original trilogy is more stated than shown.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>Snow's characterisation</h3>
      <p>Collins writes a younger Snow who is already calculating and dangerous, but the full chilling arc of his ideology requires the reader to do some work. Fiennes as an older, more controlled Snow is revelatory — he brings a bureaucratic menace that makes the character more immediately frightening than the page version at this stage of his life.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>The political argument</h3>
      <p>The novel's meditation on memory, propaganda, and manufactured consent is its most ambitious element — Collins is explicitly engaging with Hume and with how systems survive by controlling what people are allowed to remember. The film finds visual equivalents for much of this, but the essayistic passages that make the book feel genuinely political don't translate directly to screen.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>The other tributes</h3>
      <p>Collins gives the other tributes of the 50th Games more individual weight than is typical for the franchise — we know enough about them that their deaths register as losses rather than plot mechanics. The film, constrained by runtime, cannot sustain this level of characterisation across the full cast, which makes the Games themselves feel slightly less brutal than they do on the page.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>The arena spectacle</h3>
      <p>The Second Quarter Quell arena is described evocatively but experienced primarily through Haymitch's tactical mind in the novel. Lawrence's production design renders it as something visually spectacular — this is one area where the film unambiguously expands on what the book offers.</p>
    </div>

    <h2>Should You Read First?</h2>
    <p>This is one case where the order matters less than usual — both versions work as standalone experiences. That said, the book deepens the film considerably, particularly in the Snow scenes, and it's a fast read. If you're new to Panem, start with The Hunger Games and work forward. If you know the trilogy, read this one before you see the film.</p>

    <div class="verdict-box">
      <div class="verdict-title">Verdict</div>
      <p>A genuine tie — rarer than it sounds. The novel is Collins at her most politically ambitious; the film is the franchise at its most visually confident. Fiennes makes the film worth seeing regardless of whether you've read the book, but book readers will get considerably more from his scenes with Haymitch.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

<header>
  <div class="header-inner">
    <a class="site-logo" href="/">Books<span>Versus</span>Movies</a>
    <nav><a href="/">Home</a> &nbsp;&middot;&nbsp; <a href="/index_alt.html">Browse All</a> &nbsp;&middot;&nbsp; <a href="/about.html">About</a></nav>

<div class="page-hero">
  <div class="genre-tag">Science Fiction / Horror</div>
  <h1>I Am Legend</h1>
  <p class="subtitle">Book (1954) vs. Movie (2007) &mdash; dir. Francis Lawrence</p>
</div>

<div class="page-wrap">
  <div class="comparison">
    <div class="panel-book">
      <div class="panel-label">The Book</div>
      <a class="book-cover-link" href="https://amzn.to/4mbz0wg" target="_blank" rel="noopener sponsored">
        <img class="book-cover" src="./images/i-am-legend.jpg" alt="I Am Legend book cover Richard Matheson 1954" loading="lazy">
      </a>
      <a class="buy-btn" href="https://amzn.to/4mbz0wg" target="_blank" rel="noopener sponsored">Buy the Book &rarr;</a>
      <p class="affiliate-disclosure">As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="panel-film">
      <div class="panel-label">The Movie</div>
      <a class="trailer-link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dtKMEAXyPkg" target="_blank" rel="noopener">
        <div class="trailer-thumbnail">
          <img src="https://img.youtube.com/vi/dtKMEAXyPkg/maxresdefault.jpg" alt="I Am Legend 2007 film dir. Francis Lawrence official trailer">
          <div class="trailer-play">&#9658;</div>
        </div>
      </a>
      <p class="trailer-note">Starring Will Smith &mdash; Film: 2007</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="meta-strip">
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Author</strong>Richard Matheson</div>
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Book Published</strong>1954</div>
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Film Released</strong>2007</div>
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Director</strong>Francis Lawrence</div>
    <span class="verdict-badge verdict-book">Book Wins</span>
  </div>

  <div class="body-text">
    <h2>The Story in Brief</h2>
    <p>Robert Neville is the last uninfected man on Earth. A pandemic has turned the rest of humanity into vampires — creatures that gather outside his fortified house each night, calling his name, waiting. By day he hunts them. By night he drinks and tries not to go mad. Richard Matheson's 1954 novella is one of the foundational texts of modern horror — it influenced Stephen King, George Romero's zombie films, and effectively invented the post-apocalyptic survival genre. Francis Lawrence's 2007 film, with Will Smith giving one of his finest performances, grossed $585 million worldwide. It is a gripping, technically accomplished film with the wrong ending.</p>

    <h2>Key Differences</h2>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>The ending — the whole point</h3>
      <p>Matheson's novella ends with a revelation that reframes everything that came before: the vampires have developed a functioning society, and Neville — who has spent years hunting and killing them in their sleep — is the monster from their perspective. The legend of the title is what Neville has become to the new civilisation: the boogeyman, the night-stalker, the creature of nightmare. It is one of the great reversals in genre fiction. The 2007 film's theatrical ending replaces this entirely with Neville dying heroically to save survivors, turning a story about the relativity of monstrosity into a conventional sacrifice narrative. An alternate ending that is closer to Matheson's was shot but not used in the theatrical release.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>The vampires as society</h3>
      <p>Matheson's vampires are not mindless — they are frightened, organised, and building something new. The leader Ben Cortman was Neville's neighbour, and his nightly appearances outside Neville's house have a desperate human quality beneath the horror. The film's infected are rendered as purely predatory CGI creatures with no visible interiority, which makes them effective as horror but removes the novella's central argument about who deserves to survive.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>Will Smith alone</h3>
      <p>The film's considerable achievement is its extended early sequence of Smith as Neville alone in a deserted New York — hunting deer through empty streets, talking to mannequins, maintaining military discipline to avoid psychological collapse. These sequences are among the finest survival cinema of the 2000s. Smith carries the film on his presence alone, and the performance is genuinely moving in ways the script does not fully deserve.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>Neville's scientific research</h3>
      <p>The novella's Neville is an ordinary man who teaches himself biology from library books — his slow, amateur scientific work is part of the novel's texture. The film makes him a military virologist, which makes his research more conventionally credible and less interesting. The novel's Neville succeeds through persistence and ordinary intelligence; the film's through professional expertise.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>Sam the dog</h3>
      <p>Both versions feature Neville's dog — his only living companion. The film's handling of Sam's fate is the most emotionally devastating scene in either version and is more fully developed than Matheson's equivalent. This is one of the rare cases where the film invests more in a specific moment than the source, and it pays off completely.</p>
    </div>

    <h2>Should You Read First?</h2>
    <p>Yes — and read the novella specifically to experience the ending that the film removes. The theatrical cut of the 2007 film actively contradicts Matheson's argument. Read first, then watch the alternate ending version of the film rather than the theatrical cut. The novella takes two hours and contains one of genre fiction's great last lines.</p>

    <div class="verdict-box">
      <div class="verdict-title">Verdict</div>
      <p>Matheson wrote a novella with one of the great endings in horror fiction — a final inversion that reframes everything that came before. The 2007 film discards this ending entirely, replacing it with a conventional heroic conclusion that misses the point completely. Will Smith is excellent. The film is gripping. And it tells a fundamentally different story to the one Matheson wrote. Read the novella. It takes two hours and the last line will stay with you.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

<div class="page-hero">
  <div class="genre-tag">Memoir / Adventure</div>
  <h1>Into the Wild</h1>
  <p class="subtitle">Book (1996) vs. Movie (2007) &mdash; dir. Sean Penn</p>
</div>

<div class="page-wrap">
  <div class="comparison">
    <div class="panel-book">
      <div class="panel-label">The Book</div>
      <a class="book-cover-link" href="https://amzn.to/4ml6FDJ" target="_blank" rel="noopener sponsored">
        <img class="book-cover" src="./images/into-the-wild.jpg" alt="Into the Wild book cover Jon Krakauer 1996" loading="lazy">
      </a>
      <a class="buy-btn" href="https://amzn.to/4ml6FDJ" target="_blank" rel="noopener sponsored">Buy the Book &rarr;</a>
      <p class="affiliate-disclosure">As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="panel-film">
      <div class="panel-label">The Movie</div>
      <a class="trailer-link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XZG1FzyB8DI" target="_blank" rel="noopener">
        <div class="trailer-thumbnail">
          <img src="https://img.youtube.com/vi/XZG1FzyB8DI/maxresdefault.jpg" alt="Into the Wild 2007 film dir. Sean Penn official trailer">
          <div class="trailer-play">&#9658;</div>
        </div>
      </a>
      <p class="trailer-note">Starring Emile Hirsch, Marcia Gay Harden, William Hurt, Hal Holbrook &mdash; Film: 2007</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="meta-strip">
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Author</strong>Jon Krakauer</div>
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Book Published</strong>1996</div>
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Film Released</strong>2007</div>
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Director</strong>Sean Penn</div>
    <span class="verdict-badge verdict-book">Book Wins</span>
  </div>

  <div class="body-text">
    <h2>The Story in Brief</h2>
    <p>In April 1992, Christopher McCandless — twenty-four years old, recently graduated, having given his savings to charity and abandoned his car — hitchhiked to Alaska and walked alone into the wilderness. Four months later his decomposed body was found in an abandoned bus. Jon Krakauer's book, expanded from a magazine article he wrote for Outside, reconstructs McCandless's journey through his journals, the accounts of people he met along the way, and Krakauer's own investigation into the circumstances of his death. It is a work of journalism that is also a meditation on a particular kind of American idealism and its limits. Sean Penn's 2007 film, with Emile Hirsch as McCandless and Eddie Vedder's score, is beautiful, elegiac, and somewhat less honest than the source about who McCandless actually was.</p>

    <h2>Key Differences</h2>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>Krakauer's ambivalence</h3>
      <p>The book's most important quality is Krakauer's honesty about his own complicated response to McCandless — the recognition in the young man's idealism of something in himself, and the simultaneous awareness that McCandless's death was at least partly the result of arrogance and inadequate preparation. Krakauer admires and critiques in equal measure, and the book holds this tension throughout. Penn's film tilts the balance toward elegy — McCandless is presented as a noble seeker and his death as a tragedy rather than as one possible consequence of a philosophy that underestimated difficulty.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>The parallel stories</h3>
      <p>Krakauer intercuts McCandless's story with accounts of other young men who were drawn to extreme solitude and wilderness — some who survived, some who did not. This context is the book's most important structural decision: it places McCandless within a tradition of a particular kind of American idealism, showing that his journey was not unique and that its dangers were not unpredictable. The film focuses almost entirely on McCandless alone, which makes his story feel singular rather than representative.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>Emile Hirsch's performance</h3>
      <p>Hirsch lost significant weight for the role and gives a committed, physically demanding performance. His McCandless is intelligent, warm, and genuinely compelling in his certainty — you understand why people were drawn to him. This is the film's great achievement: making McCandless's appeal felt rather than explained. The book renders his appeal through the accounts of those who met him; Hirsch renders it directly, and the directness is more immediately persuasive.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>The supporting characters</h3>
      <p>The people McCandless met on his journey — Wayne Westerberg, Jan Burres and Bob, the octogenarian Ron Franz — are rendered with particular care in the film, and Hal Holbrook's Franz is quietly devastating. The book gives these characters more space and more reflection; the film gives them more emotional immediacy. Both approaches illuminate the loneliness of a man who was loved by everyone he met briefly and could not sustain connection with anyone permanently.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>The cause of death</h3>
      <p>Krakauer investigates the cause of McCandless's death with journalistic rigour — his theory, involving the toxic seeds of wild potato plants, has been both supported and contested by subsequent research. The book's engagement with this question gives McCandless's death a specific cause and thus a slightly different moral valence than Penn's film, which is somewhat more ambiguous about what exactly killed him and more interested in the symbolic dimensions of his end.</p>
    </div>

    <h2>Should You Read First?</h2>
    <p>Yes — Krakauer's ambivalence is the book's essential quality and the film's comparative romanticism means watching first will give you a version of the story that the book then complicates. Read first for the full picture — the journalism, the parallel stories, Krakauer's honest self-implication — and the film becomes a beautiful, elegiac companion that chooses feeling over scrutiny. Both choices are defensible. Krakauer's is more honest.</p>

    <div class="verdict-box">
      <div class="verdict-title">Verdict</div>
      <p>Krakauer wrote a work of journalism that holds McCandless's idealism and its consequences in honest tension — admiring and critical simultaneously. Penn made a beautiful film that tips toward elegy and away from scrutiny. The book is the more complete account of what happened and why it matters. The film is more immediately moving and less intellectually honest. Read the book for the truth. See the film for Hirsch and the Alaskan light. The book wins because it is braver.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

<div class="page-hero">
  <div class="genre-tag">Romance / Drama</div>
  <h1>It Ends With Us</h1>
  <p class="subtitle">Book (2016) vs. Movie (2024) &mdash; dir. Justin Baldoni</p>
</div>
<div class="page-wrap">
  <div class="comparison">
    <div class="panel-book">
      <div class="panel-label">The Book</div>
      <a class="book-cover-link" href="https://amzn.to/4mk8AIH" target="_blank" rel="noopener sponsored">
        <img class="book-cover" src="./images/it-ends-with-us.jpg" alt="It Ends With Us book cover Colleen Hoover 2016" loading="lazy">
      </a>
      <a class="buy-btn" href="https://amzn.to/4mk8AIH" target="_blank" rel="noopener sponsored">Buy the Book &rarr;</a>
      <p class="affiliate-disclosure">As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="panel-film">
      <div class="panel-label">The Movie</div>
      <a class="trailer-link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DLET_u31M4M" target="_blank" rel="noopener">
        <div class="trailer-thumbnail">
          <img src="https://img.youtube.com/vi/DLET_u31M4M/maxresdefault.jpg" alt="It Ends With Us 2024 film official trailer">
          <div class="trailer-play">&#9658;</div>
        </div>
      </a>
      <p class="trailer-note">Starring Blake Lively, Justin Baldoni, Brandon Sklenar &mdash; Film: 2024</p>
    </div>
  </div>
  <div class="meta-strip">
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Author</strong>Colleen Hoover</div>
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Book Published</strong>2016</div>
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Film Released</strong>2024</div>
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Director</strong>Justin Baldoni</div>
    <span class="verdict-badge verdict-book">Book Wins</span>
  </div>
  <div class="body-text">
    <h2>The Story in Brief</h2>
    <p>Lily Bloom moves to Boston, starts a flower shop, and falls for Ryle Kincaid — a neurosurgeon who is intense, charming, and eventually abusive. A first love, Atlas Corrigan, re-enters her life. Colleen Hoover's novel is a romance that becomes something more serious — a frank examination of domestic abuse cycles and the difficulty of leaving. The 2024 film, directed by Justin Baldoni and starring Blake Lively, grossed over three hundred and fifty million dollars worldwide and arrived amid significant off-screen controversy between its director and star. The novel remains the cleaner experience.</p>
    <h2>Key Differences</h2>
    
    <div class="difference">
      <h3>Lily's interiority</h3>
      <p>Hoover writes Lily's experience of the abuse with specificity and psychological honesty — the rationalisation, the love that coexists with the fear, the particular way each incident is explained away. This interior process is the novel's most important material and it is difficult to externalise on screen. The film shows the incidents; the novel shows the thinking that surrounds them.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>The off-screen controversy</h3>
      <p>The film's production and release were overshadowed by publicised conflict between Blake Lively and Justin Baldoni, which made it impossible to watch the finished film without awareness of the friction behind it. The novel exists outside this context. Whether the controversy is relevant to the film's meaning is a matter of genuine debate.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>Blake Lively as Lily</h3>
      <p>Lively commits fully to the role but her star quality — her physical confidence, her innate glamour — works slightly against the novel's Lily, who is more ordinary and more visibly uncertain. The film's Lily is more immediately sympathetic; the novel's is more complicated.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>Ryle Kincaid</h3>
      <p>Justin Baldoni plays Ryle — the abusive partner — in his own film, which creates an obvious tension. The novel's Ryle is rendered through Lily's perception, which means his appeal is established before his violence. The film makes his appeal and his menace somewhat harder to balance.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>The journal sections</h3>
      <p>Hoover uses Lily's teenage journal entries — letters to Ellen DeGeneres — to establish her backstory and her relationship with Atlas. These sections provide context the film must deliver through other means. The film handles this efficiently but loses the specific voice of the teenage Lily.</p>
    </div>
    <h2>Should You Read First?</h2>
    <p>Yes — the novel's interior handling of the abuse cycle is its most important quality and the film cannot fully replicate it. Read first to understand what Hoover is doing, then see the film as a separate interpretation of the same material.</p>
    <div class="verdict-box">
      <div class="verdict-title">Verdict</div>
      <p>Hoover wrote a novel that takes domestic abuse seriously inside a romance structure and does so with genuine skill. Baldoni made a film that arrived in difficult circumstances and is a lesser version of that novel. The book is the original. The film is an adaptation that serves the story less well than the source. Read the novel.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

<div class="page-hero">
  <div class="genre-tag">Gothic Romance / Classic</div>
  <h1>Jane Eyre</h1>
  <p class="subtitle">Book (1847) vs. Movie (2011) &mdash; dir. Cary Joji Fukunaga</p>
</div>
<div class="page-wrap">
  <div class="comparison">
    <div class="panel-book">
      <div class="panel-label">The Book</div>
      <a class="book-cover-link" href="https://amzn.to/41ecrxf" target="_blank" rel="noopener sponsored">
        <img class="book-cover" src="./images/jane-eyre.jpg" alt="Jane Eyre book cover Charlotte Brontë 1847" loading="lazy">
      </a>
      <a class="buy-btn" href="https://amzn.to/41ecrxf" target="_blank" rel="noopener sponsored">Buy the Book &rarr;</a>
      <p class="affiliate-disclosure">As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="panel-film">
      <div class="panel-label">The Movie</div>
      <a class="trailer-link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8IFsdfk3mlk" target="_blank" rel="noopener">
        <div class="trailer-thumbnail">
          <img src="https://img.youtube.com/vi/8IFsdfk3mlk/maxresdefault.jpg" alt="Jane Eyre 2011 film official trailer">
          <div class="trailer-play">&#9658;</div>
        </div>
      </a>
      <p class="trailer-note">Starring Mia Wasikowska, Michael Fassbender &mdash; Film: 2011</p>
    </div>
  </div>
  <div class="meta-strip">
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Author</strong>Charlotte Brontë</div>
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Book Published</strong>1847</div>
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Film Released</strong>2011</div>
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Director</strong>Cary Joji Fukunaga</div>
    <span class="verdict-badge verdict-book">Book Wins</span>
  </div>
  <div class="body-text">
    <h2>The Story in Brief</h2>
    <p>Jane Eyre is an orphan who survives a brutal charity school to become governess at Thornfield Hall, where she falls in love with the brooding, morally complicated Edward Rochester. Charlotte Brontë's 1847 novel is narrated in Jane's first person — direct, passionate, and morally certain in a way that was radical for its time. Cary Joji Fukunaga's 2011 film, with Mia Wasikowska and Michael Fassbender, is the finest screen adaptation of the novel yet made. It is still a reduction of a work that lives in its voice.</p>
    <h2>Key Differences</h2>
    
    <div class="difference">
      <h3>Jane's voice</h3>
      <p>Brontë's Jane addresses the reader directly — "Reader, I married him" is the most famous instance of a sustained intimacy that runs throughout the novel. Jane's narration is the experience: her specific moral intelligence, her refusal to be patronised, her way of seeing the world with absolute clarity. Wasikowska's performance is excellent and communicates much of this through expression and bearing. She cannot communicate the sentences.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>Michael Fassbender's Rochester</h3>
      <p>Fassbender plays Rochester with a barely contained volatility that captures the character's essential quality — the darkness that Jane sees and loves in full knowledge of what it is. This is one of the great casting decisions in literary adaptation. The novel's Rochester is rendered entirely through Jane's perception, which gives him a complexity the film slightly simplifies by showing him directly.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>Fukunaga's visual language</h3>
      <p>The film opens in medias res — Jane fleeing across the moors — before moving back to tell the story. Fukunaga's cinematography gives Thornfield Hall a Gothic weight that matches the novel's atmosphere. The Yorkshire landscape becomes a moral landscape in both versions, though the novel's language and the film's images achieve this through entirely different means.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>The attic and Bertha Mason</h3>
      <p>The novel gives Bertha Mason — Rochester's imprisoned first wife — more presence and more ambiguity. She is a figure of terror and also of kinship with Jane; their situations as women are not entirely different. The film handles Bertha efficiently but cannot sustain the novel's more disturbing parallels.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>The novel's length</h3>
      <p>Brontë's novel is substantial and covers Jane's full childhood — the abuse at Gateshead, the years at Lowood, the slow development of her character before Thornfield. The film compresses the early sections to reach Thornfield faster, which is cinematically necessary and means you meet Jane as a formed person rather than watching her form.</p>
    </div>
    <h2>Should You Read First?</h2>
    <p>Yes — Jane's voice is the novel and no film can render it. Read first and Wasikowska's performance becomes the finest possible visual gloss on what Brontë put on the page. Watch first and you'll know the story without the experience that makes the story matter.</p>
    <div class="verdict-box">
      <div class="verdict-title">Verdict</div>
      <p>Brontë wrote one of the great first-person novels in English literature — Jane's voice is its own argument, its own world. Fukunaga made the finest adaptation yet and it remains considerably less than the novel. Read Jane Eyre. See the film for Fassbender. The book is the thing.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

<div class="page-hero">
  <div class="genre-tag">Science Fiction / Adventure</div>
  <h1>Jurassic Park</h1>
  <p class="subtitle">Book (1990) vs. Movie (1993) &mdash; dir. Steven Spielberg</p>
</div>
<div class="page-wrap">
  <div class="comparison">
    <div class="panel-book">
      <div class="panel-label">The Book</div>
      <a class="book-cover-link" href="https://amzn.to/4c4szGF" target="_blank" rel="noopener sponsored">
        <img class="book-cover" src="./images/jurassic-park.jpg" alt="Jurassic Park book cover Michael Crichton 1990" loading="lazy">
      </a>
      <a class="buy-btn" href="https://amzn.to/4c4szGF" target="_blank" rel="noopener sponsored">Buy the Book &rarr;</a>
      <p class="affiliate-disclosure">As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="panel-film">
      <div class="panel-label">The Movie</div>
      <a class="trailer-link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QWBKEmWWL38" target="_blank" rel="noopener">
        <div class="trailer-thumbnail">
          <img src="https://img.youtube.com/vi/QWBKEmWWL38/maxresdefault.jpg" alt="Jurassic Park 1993 film official trailer">
          <div class="trailer-play">&#9658;</div>
        </div>
      </a>
      <p class="trailer-note">Starring Sam Neill, Laura Dern, Jeff Goldblum &mdash; Film: 1993</p>
    </div>
  </div>
  <div class="meta-strip">
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Author</strong>Michael Crichton</div>
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Book Published</strong>1990</div>
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Film Released</strong>1993</div>
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Director</strong>Steven Spielberg</div>
    <span class="verdict-badge verdict-book">Book Wins</span>
  </div>
  <div class="body-text">
    <h2>The Story in Brief</h2>
    <p>Billionaire John Hammond has cloned dinosaurs from ancient DNA and built a theme park on a Costa Rican island. When the park's systems fail, a handful of scientists and Hammond's grandchildren must survive. Michael Crichton's novel is a serious work of scientific speculation wrapped in a thriller — darker, more intellectually rigorous, and considerably less sentimental than what Spielberg made of it. Spielberg's film is one of the most thrilling cinema experiences of the 1990s.</p>
    <h2>Key Differences</h2>
    
    <div class="difference">
      <h3>Ian Malcolm's chaos theory</h3>
      <p>Crichton gives Malcolm extended lectures on chaos theory, complexity, and the arrogance of scientific hubris — passages that are genuinely interesting and form the novel's intellectual spine. The film reduces Malcolm's arguments to memorable one-liners.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>Tone and darkness</h3>
      <p>Crichton's novel is substantially darker than Spielberg's film — more characters die, more graphically, and the horror of what Hammond has done is more unambiguously condemned. Spielberg sentimentalises Hammond into a well-meaning eccentric rather than the novel's genuinely culpable megalomaniac.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>The dinosaurs</h3>
      <p>Spielberg's dinosaurs are one of cinema's great achievements — the initial appearance of the brachiosaurus is still breathtaking thirty years later. The film makes you feel the scale, the reality, the extraordinary wrongness of a living dinosaur. This is the area where the film most clearly surpasses the source.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>The children</h3>
      <p>The novel's children are more actively involved in understanding what's happening and less purely there to be rescued. The film reduces them to conventional thriller children.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>Hammond's fate</h3>
      <p>In the novel, Hammond is killed by a pack of small dinosaurs — the ones he dismissed as irrelevant. This is a piece of thematic precision that the film cuts entirely, giving Hammond a sentimental exit.</p>
    </div>
    <h2>Should You Read First?</h2>
    <p>Yes — specifically to get the novel's darker, more intellectually serious version before Spielberg's magnificent but somewhat defanged blockbuster replaces it.</p>
    <div class="verdict-box">
      <div class="verdict-title">Verdict</div>
      <p>Spielberg made one of cinema's great experiences and Crichton wrote a better, darker book. The film's dinosaurs are irreplaceable; the novel's argument is irreplaceable. See the film for the experience. Read the novel to understand what the experience was originally about.</p>
    </div>
  </div>
  <div class="related-section">
    <h3>More Comparisons</h3>

  <div class="header-inner">

<div class="page-hero">
  <div class="genre-tag">Literary Fiction / Drama</div>
  <h1>The Kite Runner</h1>
  <p class="subtitle">Book (2003) vs. Movie (2007) &mdash; dir. Marc Forster</p>
</div>

<div class="page-wrap">
  <div class="comparison">
    <div class="panel-book">
      <div class="panel-label">The Book</div>
      <a class="book-cover-link" href="https://amzn.to/41Jy7RY" target="_blank" rel="noopener sponsored">
        <img class="book-cover" src="./images/kite-runner.jpg" alt="The Kite Runner book cover Khaled Hosseini 2003" loading="lazy">
      </a>
      <a class="buy-btn" href="https://amzn.to/41Jy7RY" target="_blank" rel="noopener sponsored">Buy the Book &rarr;</a>
      <p class="affiliate-disclosure">As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="panel-film">
      <div class="panel-label">The Movie</div>
      <a class="trailer-link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sLtavGjAOJY" target="_blank" rel="noopener">
        <div class="trailer-thumbnail">
          <img src="https://img.youtube.com/vi/sLtavGjAOJY/maxresdefault.jpg" alt="The Kite Runner 2007 film dir. Marc Forster official trailer">
          <div class="trailer-play">▶</div>
        </div>
      </a>
      <p class="trailer-note">Starring Khalid Abdalla, Homayoun Ershadi, Zekeria Ebrahimi</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="meta-strip">
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Author</strong>Khaled Hosseini</div>
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Book Published</strong>2003</div>
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Film Released</strong>2007</div>
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Director</strong>Marc Forster</div>
    <span class="verdict-badge verdict-book">Book Wins</span>
  </div>

  <div class="body-text">
    <h2>The Story in Brief</h2>
    <p>Amir grows up in Kabul in the 1970s, the privileged son of a wealthy Pashtun man, with Hassan as his closest companion &mdash; a Hazara boy who is his father's servant and, though neither knows it yet, his half-brother. When Amir witnesses Hassan's assault and does nothing, the guilt defines the rest of his life. The story follows Amir from Kabul to California, and eventually back to a Taliban-controlled Afghanistan, in search of a redemption he may not deserve. Khaled Hosseini's debut novel sold tens of millions of copies and introduced many Western readers to Afghan history and culture. Marc Forster's adaptation is sincere and handsomely made, and it cannot carry the novel's full emotional weight.</p>

    <h2>Key Differences</h2>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>Amir's guilt and self-loathing</h3>
      <p>The novel is narrated entirely by Amir, and Hosseini gives him one of the most forensically honest interior voices in popular fiction. Amir doesn't just feel guilty &mdash; he understands exactly why he did what he did, catalogues his own cowardice with painful clarity, and spends decades constructing elaborate self-justifications that he then dismantles. The film can show his behaviour but not his internal accounting. Khalid Abdalla is a capable and sympathetic presence, but the film loses the queasy intimacy of being locked inside a narrator who knows he's a coward and tells you so anyway.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>Hassan's presence</h3>
      <p>In the novel, Hassan is rendered with great tenderness &mdash; his loyalty, his dignity, his simple goodness are established across years of shared childhood before the assault. Hosseini takes his time. The film compresses their friendship into a handful of scenes, which means the central betrayal, while still affecting, doesn't carry quite the accumulated weight it does on the page. You need to love Hassan before you can fully feel what Amir's failure costs.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>Afghanistan as setting</h3>
      <p>One of the novel's great achievements is its portrait of Kabul before and after the Soviet invasion and Taliban rule &mdash; a city of kite tournaments, pomegranate trees, and ordinary life that most Western readers had never encountered. Hosseini's Afghanistan is vivid and specific in a way that makes its destruction feel like a genuine loss. The film captures this visually, shot largely in China standing in for Afghanistan, but the texture of daily life that Hosseini builds through prose &mdash; the smells, the sounds, the social fabric &mdash; is necessarily thinner on screen.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>Baba's character</h3>
      <p>Amir's father Baba is one of Hosseini's richest creations &mdash; a man of tremendous charisma and genuine moral seriousness who has nonetheless committed a betrayal of his own that mirrors and explains Amir's. The novel has room to establish him fully: his contradictions, his disappointments, his fierce love. The film gives Homayoun Ershadi the material to suggest this, but Baba's full complexity is compressed. His trajectory from Kabul patriarch to San Jose gas station attendant is the novel's most quietly devastating thread.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>Sohrab's trauma</h3>
      <p>The novel's final third, in which Amir attempts to rescue Hassan's son Sohrab from Taliban captivity and then navigate the boy's profound psychological damage, is handled with care and patience. Sohrab's near-suicide and his long silence afterward are given the space they need. The film rushes through this section to reach its resolution, and the emotional recovery feels abbreviated &mdash; the kite-flying ending lands, but it earns less of its catharsis than the novel does.</p>
    </div>

    <h2>Should You Read First?</h2>
    <p>Yes &mdash; this is a novel that works primarily through interiority and accumulated time, two things film handles poorly. The film is a reasonable companion piece and a sincere adaptation, but it was always going to struggle with a story whose power comes from being trapped inside a guilty conscience for four hundred pages. Read the book and you'll feel the ending's redemption properly. Watch the film first and the ending will still move you, but you won't fully understand what it cost to get there.</p>

    <div class="verdict-box">
      <div class="verdict-title">Verdict</div>
      <p>Forster's film is earnest, well-intentioned, and ultimately a lesser version of a great novel. The Kite Runner works on the page because Hosseini gives you no distance from Amir's shame &mdash; you're inside it for the entire book, and the redemption feels earned because you've lived the guilt alongside him. The film shows you a man seeking redemption; the novel makes you seek it with him. Read the book. The film is fine. The book is the one that stays.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

<header>
  <div class="header-inner">

<div class="page-hero">
  <div class="genre-tag">Crime / Noir</div>
  <h1>LA Confidential</h1>
  <p class="subtitle">Book (1990) vs. Movie (1997) &mdash; dir. Curtis Hanson</p>
</div>
<div class="page-wrap">
  <div class="comparison">
    <div class="panel-book">
      <div class="panel-label">The Book</div>
      <a class="book-cover-link" href="https://amzn.to/4tvZDys" target="_blank" rel="noopener sponsored">
        <img class="book-cover" src="./images/la-confidential.jpg" alt="LA Confidential book cover James Ellroy 1990" loading="lazy">
      </a>
      <a class="buy-btn" href="https://amzn.to/4tvZDys" target="_blank" rel="noopener sponsored">Buy the Book &rarr;</a>
      <p class="affiliate-disclosure">As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="panel-film">
      <div class="panel-label">The Movie</div>
      <a class="trailer-link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6sOXrY5yV4g" target="_blank" rel="noopener">
        <div class="trailer-thumbnail">
          <img src="https://img.youtube.com/vi/6sOXrY5yV4g/maxresdefault.jpg" alt="LA Confidential 1997 film official trailer">
          <div class="trailer-play">&#9658;</div>
        </div>
      </a>
      <p class="trailer-note">Starring Kevin Spacey, Russell Crowe, Guy Pearce, Kim Basinger &mdash; Film: 1997</p>
    </div>
  </div>
  <div class="meta-strip">
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Author</strong>James Ellroy</div>
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Book Published</strong>1990</div>
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Film Released</strong>1997</div>
    <div class="meta-item"><strong>Director</strong>Curtis Hanson</div>
    <span class="verdict-badge verdict-tie">Too Close to Call</span>
  </div>
  <div class="body-text">
    <h2>The Story in Brief</h2>
    <p>Three Los Angeles detectives in the early 1950s — the straight-arrow Ed Exley, the brutal Bud White, and the celebrity-fixated Jack Vincennes — become entangled in a conspiracy that runs from a Nite Owl coffee shop massacre through the LAPD's own corruption to the upper reaches of Hollywood and organised crime. James Ellroy's novel is six hundred pages of dense, compressed, telegraphic prose — one of the great American crime novels. Curtis Hanson's film won two Academy Awards and is one of the finest crime films of the 1990s. This is a genuine standoff.</p>
    <h2>Key Differences</h2>
    
    <div class="difference">
      <h3>Ellroy's prose style</h3>
      <p>Ellroy writes in a clipped, staccato style that strips out connective tissue and drops the reader directly into sensation and action. The novel is dense and demands concentration. Hanson's film translates this density into visual compression — many scenes, rapid cuts, maximum information. Both approaches achieve the same effect through different means.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>The novel's scope</h3>
      <p>Ellroy's novel is considerably longer and wider than the film. Several significant subplots — including a substantial thread involving a character called Dudley Smith's relationship with the Mexican mob — are condensed or removed. The film makes these cuts intelligently but the novel's world is larger.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>The three detectives</h3>
      <p>Ellroy gives all three protagonists roughly equal weight and interiority. Hanson's film slightly favours Exley (Guy Pearce) and White (Russell Crowe), making Vincennes (Kevin Spacey) more peripheral. All three performances are exceptional.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>Kim Basinger</h3>
      <p>Basinger won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress as Lynn Bracken, the Veronica Lake lookalike. Her performance gives the film a romantic and melancholy centre that the novel, more interested in its male detectives, doesn't quite have. This is one of the rare instances where the film adds something the source lacks.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="difference">
      <h3>The resolution</h3>
      <p>Both versions arrive at the same destination — the conspiracy revealed, the corrupted institution partially reformed, the surviving detective carrying the weight of what he's done. The film's resolution is somewhat cleaner. The novel's is more morally complicated.</p>
    </div>
    <h2>Should You Read First?</h2>
    <p>Either order works genuinely well. The film is so accomplished that watching first is a legitimate choice — you'll then read the novel with the three detectives fully realised in your imagination. Reading first gives you the full scope of Ellroy's world before Hanson necessarily narrows it.</p>
    <div class="verdict-box">
      <div class="verdict-title">Verdict</div>
      <p>Ellroy wrote one of the great American crime novels and Hanson made one of the great American crime films. They are different achievements at different scales. The novel is more ambitious. The film is more perfectly constructed. Read both. This is one of the very few genuine ties.</p>
    </div>
  </div>
